items.title: Montage
items.reason: The 119-120-minute South Korean kidnapping mystery links an unresolved child abduction to a seemingly identical crime fifteen years later. A flower left at the old crime scene and captured on a traffic camera creates a fresh lead just before the statute of limitations expires. After a new child disappears, the retired investigator notices inconsistencies in the apparently straightforward case and disputes his colleagues' premature conclusion. Flashbacks, conflicting evidence and the suspicious grandfather gradually connect the two crimes. The later disclosures identify the grandfather as the original abductor and the bereaved mother as the person who recreated the kidnapping to force a confession; the original death and the motive are explained at the end. These clues and changing suspicions provide genuine investigation and some mid-story reframing, but the most decisive answers remain late. Modern Korean Cinema explicitly describes a leisurely pace and deliberate withholding of information, while AsianMovieWeb praises the coherent twists and suspense but notes familiar genre devices and occasional implausible police handling of evidence. The film therefore rates more strongly for mystery and clue work than for nonstop revelation or action. Its grief and revenge dilemma are substantial without turning it into primarily a relationship drama.

items.title: Strange Darling
items.reason: This 96-minute psychological crime thriller is presented as six chapters in the order 3, 5, 1, 4, 2, 6, followed by an epilogue. It first shows a wounded woman fleeing an armed man, then revisits their motel encounter and the farmhouse pursuit from earlier moments. Incremental contextual changes initially undermine the viewer's assumptions; the central revelation in Chapter 2 establishes that the apparent victim is the serial murderer and that her pursuer is a police officer. Chapter 6 then tests that new understanding as she stages herself as a victim to manipulate arriving officers and escape. These are consequential perspective reversals, but the biggest explanatory turn occurs roughly an hour in, after which the remaining story becomes more linear survival and pursuit; do not mistake uninterrupted danger for uninterrupted new answers. The Washington Post praises the taut cat-and-mouse structure and striking 35mm cinematography. Bloody Disgusting praises the early surprises but finds the last chapter comparatively predictable; The Guardian calls the retro-slasher construction too conspicuously tricksy. The film has high deception, unreliable perspective, suspense and brutality, with little conventional evidence-gathering, no broad conspiracy, and a deliberately retro aesthetic that is separate from its polished visual craft.
